blocks.title: Executive summary
blocks.content:
Executive summary
Introduction
A home-based record is a health document used 
to record the history of health services received 
by an individual. It is kept in the household, 
in either paper or electronic format, by the 
individual or their caregiver and is intended to 
be integrated into the health information system 
and complement records maintained by health 
facilities. They range from antenatal notes or 
vaccination-only cards, progressing to more 
expanded vaccination-plus cards, child health 
books or integrated maternal and child health 
books, which often include health education

summary.text: Summarises the WHO guideline on home-based records, defining them as household-kept paper or electronic health documents ranging from vaccination cards to integrated maternal and child health books, whose benefits had not been systematically reviewed. It outlines development under the WHO handbook process with GRADE and an evidence-to-decision framework, and presents two recommendations: using home-based records to complement facility records, and that evidence is insufficient to favour any particular type or design. It also lists remarks on low-certainty evidence, privacy of HIV information, sustainable financing and further research needs.

blocks.title: Home-based records: an overview
blocks.content:
1. Home-based records: an overview
1.1 Functions of home-based records
A home-based record is a health document used 
to record the history of health services received 
by an individual. Its primary purpose is to record 
essential information related to maternal, 
newborn and child health (MNCH), including 
health status, visits to a health care provider, 
vaccinations received and the child’s growth 
and development. A home-based record is 
kept in the household, in either paper or 
electronic format, for use by the woman 
for maternal health and/or by the caregiver 
of the household’s newbor

summary.text: Gives an overview of home-based records, describing their purpose in recording maternal, newborn and child health care and the different types in use, from maternal records and vaccination cards to integrated MCH books. It discusses their functions and global use and introduces the rationale and scope of the guideline. It ends by explaining how the priority questions and proximal and distal outcomes were chosen.

blocks.title: Methods
blocks.content:
They comprised academics with expertise in 
guideline development, research or policy 
development related to home-based records, as 
well as international and country-level policy-
makers and implementers of home-based record 
programmes. This diverse group was drawn from 
every WHO region, and efforts were made to 
ensure geographic representation and gender 
balance, and that they had no important conflicts 
of interest. 
An initial scoping meeting was held in Geneva 
in December 2016 and contributed to the 
identification of priority questions and outcomes for 
the guideline (participants

summary.text: Describes how the guideline was developed according to the WHO handbook, including the roles of the WHO Steering Group, the 12-member Guideline Development Group, the Technical Working Group and external partners. It covers declarations of interest and the December 2016 scoping meeting that set six priority questions and outcomes. It explains evidence retrieval through systematic reviews, a qualitative evidence synthesis and a framework analysis of grey literature and key informant interviews, with certainty grading. It closes with the categories used for recommendations and the process of document preparation and peer review.

blocks.title: Recommendations and evidence on home-based records for MNCH
blocks.content:
3. Recommendations and evidence 
on home-based records for MNCH
3.1 Recommendations
Following the method outlined in section 2, the GDG put forward the following recommendations (Table 3).
Table 3. Recommendations on home-based records
Recommendations 
1.	 The use of home-based records is recommended for the care of pregnant women, mothers, newborns and 
children, to complement facility-based records, to improve care-seeking behaviours, male involvement 
and support in the household, maternal and child home care practices, infant and child feeding, and 
communication between health providers a

summary.text: Presents the two recommendations on home-based records, with the rationale that although evidence certainty was low and studies were few, old and varied, benefits outweighed harms given positive effects on several care-seeking, home care and communication outcomes and use in at least 163 countries. It reviews the quantitative and qualitative evidence for each priority question, including values, acceptability, equity, resources and feasibility. Remarks address design, privacy and sustainable financing. The section ends with the evidence-to-decision framework table rating effects, certainty, costs, equity, acceptability and feasibility.

blocks.title: Implementation considerations
blocks.content:
Implementation considerations were derived 
from the framework analysis and were discussed 
within the GDG. Broadly, these deal with the 
content and design of home-based records, 
integration into health services and systems, costs, 
and addressing the needs of health workers, 
women and caregivers. 
The GDG emphasized that every stage of the 
implementation process, from design to the 
training of providers to utilization by end-users, 
should be planned and funded, as each stage can 
affect the home-based record’s potential impact 
on outcomes. These considerations may apply to 
national an

summary.text: Sets out implementation considerations for home-based records, stressing planning and funding at every stage, government ownership, stakeholder involvement and harmonised content across health areas. It advises local adaptation and testing, design for low literacy, regular redesigns and attention to privacy. It also notes concerns about advertising on records and points to the Framework of Engagement with Non-State Actors for weighing risks.

blocks.title: Research gaps
blocks.content:
During the guideline development process, the 
GDG identified gaps that need to be addressed 
in future research:
1.	 More research is needed on the impact of 
home-based records on MNCH and health 
service outcomes. The evidence available 
is limited; of low confidence; some studies 
are from before 2000; and almost half were 
conducted in high-income countries. 
2.	 Home-based records were initially implemented 
to support caregivers or health systems. The 
content of these records and their use has 
changed and, in some cases, become more 
complex. Evaluations have used a broad range 
of ou

summary.text: Lists research gaps on home-based records, including the need for more and better-quality studies on health outcomes, standardised outcome measures and a logic model. It calls for research on effects on providers, comparisons of formats and electronic records, and cost-effectiveness of integrated records. It also identifies implementation questions such as design, durability, free versus paid distribution and incentive schemes.

blocks.title: Planned dissemination of this guideline
blocks.content:
6. Planned dissemination  
of this guideline 
Following the GDG consensus meeting in 
November 2017 in Geneva, a further two-day 
meeting was held. This brought together some 
GDG members, WHO staff from Geneva and 
regional offices, and representatives of UN 
agencies and international partner organizations. 
The purpose was to discuss the priorities for home-
based records going forward, decide what country 
support will be needed for implementation of 
this guideline, and map out the entry points 
for its dissemination. Different products for 
different audiences were discussed, including t

summary.text: Describes a meeting after the November 2017 consensus meeting to plan dissemination, which identified priorities such as a global coordinating platform, monitoring, training materials and harmonised research.

blocks.title: Updating of the guideline
blocks.content:
It is anticipated that an update would be 
appropriate five years after publication (2023), 
unless significant new evidence emerges in the 
meantime. This time frame will allow new and 
updated practice, evaluations and research to 
be taken into account. In accordance with the 
process for updating WHO guidelines, the WHO 
Steering Group will continue to monitor research 
developments around home-based records, 
particularly in relation to questions for which 
no evidence was found and those supported by 
low-quality evidence. 
Towards the end of the five-year period, 
the relevance of the g

summary.text: States that the guideline is expected to be updated in 2023 unless important new evidence emerges, with the Steering Group monitoring research and running a new scoping review near the end of that period.

summary.text: Annex 5, detailing the evidence on effects of home-based records for each priority question, beginning with maternal care-seeking, care practices and morbidity in cluster trials of maternal and child health handbooks in Mongolia and Indonesia. It continues with newborn and child outcomes and with health service outcomes such as satisfaction and women's sense of control when holding their own notes, drawing on trials in the United Kingdom and Australia. Most effects are small or non-significant, with a few positive findings such as tetanus immunization, and certainty ranges from very low to moderate. The block ends with a list of names used for such records in different countries and WHO contact details.
